planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Graffiti was bred for a compact, uniform, early-flowering habit better suited to bedding and container use than taller, later-blooming seed-grown pentas.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, and expect a compact, floriferous plant that begins blooming quickly and continues nonstop through the hottest part of summer. Graffiti is a vegetatively propagated pentas series bred for a smaller, more uniform, earlier-flowering habit than older seed-grown pentas, producing dense clusters of small, star-shaped flowers in red, pink, lavender, or white that are outstanding at drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout the growing season. Its compact size makes it especially well suited to container plantings, small beds, and mass landscape use where a shorter, tidier plant is preferred over taller pentas selections. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom, and the plant tolerates heat and humidity with ease, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South pollinator gardens through summer's peak.
sources: Proven Winners and Selecta — Graffiti pentas series notes

common_name: Black Pearl Ornamental Pepper (Near-Black Foliage Award-Winning Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; Black Pearl is grown primarily as an ornamental for its striking near-black foliage and fruit rather than for culinary heat, though the small round peppers are technically edible and quite hot.

directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Pearl won the All-America Selections award in 2006 for its dramatic, glossy, near-black foliage and abundant small, round, pearl-like fruit that emerges black and ripens through deep red, creating a striking, ever-changing color display on a single compact plant that works as well in a decorative container or mixed bed as it does in a vegetable garden. The fruit carries substantial heat, comparable to a cayenne pepper, and while edible it is grown mainly for ornamental impact rather than as a culinary crop. Its dark foliage provides dramatic color contrast against silver or chartreuse companion plants, and the compact, well-branched habit needs no staking or special care beyond routine watering and feeding.
sources: All-America Selections — Black Pearl pepper 2006 winner notes

common_name: Chilly Chili Pepper (Heatless Kid-Friendly Ornamental Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; Chilly Chili is bred specifically to lack capsaicin, the compound responsible for pepper heat, making it safe to grow around children who may be tempted to pick and taste the colorful fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Chilly Chili won an All-America Selections award as the first heatless ornamental pepper, bred to eliminate capsaicin entirely so its abundant small, slender, upright fruit — which ripens through a colorful progression of purple, yellow, orange, and red, often several colors present on the plant at once — can be safely tasted by curious children without any burning heat. Its compact, tidy habit and long-lasting, weather-resistant fruit display make it an excellent choice for children's gardens, containers, and edging where the bright, changing fruit color provides months of interest from summer through fall. Because the fruit holds its color and shape well after ripening, plants often remain colorful and attractive right up until frost.
sources: All-America Selections — Chilly Chili pepper winner notes

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant container plants after the last frost in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Kong series was bred specifically for shade, producing some of the largest coleus leaves available, and needs protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the oversized foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep soil consistently moist, since the Kong series' enormous leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions. Kong Rose is part of the Kong coleus series, bred for exceptionally large, heart-shaped leaves — often 6–8 inches across, among the biggest of any coleus — in a rich rose-pink center bordered by a broad green margin, creating bold, tropical-looking color in the shade garden or a large container. Its compact, mounding habit and huge leaf size make a dramatic textural statement massed in a shaded bed or as a single specimen in a large pot, pairing well with ferns, hostas, and other big-leaved shade perennials. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into leaf growth rather than seed production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a fuller, bushier habit.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Kong coleus series notes

common_name: Dolce Heuchera (Compact Colorful Coral Bells Series)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Dolce heuchera develops its richest foliage color with some morning sun but needs protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves in Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with morning sun for the best foliage color, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. Dolce is a heuchera breeding series bred for compact, uniform habit and an especially wide range of rich, saturated foliage colors — from near-black and deep wine-purple to caramel, lime, and silvery-blue — that hold their color well through the growing season, topped by airy sprays of small pink to white flowers in late spring that attract hummingbirds. Its tidy, well-behaved clumps make it a reliable choice for the front of a shaded border, mass plantings, or containers, and the wide color range allows striking combinations when several Dolce selections are planted together. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, and remove tattered winter foliage in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: Proven Winners — Dolce heuchera series notes
